subject: Operating Systems
title: CPU Scheduling (SJF, RR, FCFS)
description: How the OS picks the next process: arrival, burst, waiting and turnaround math.
intro: Scheduling decides order of execution. GATE tests whether you can build a Gantt chart and compute waiting/turnaround without mixing them up.
concept: For each process: completion − arrival = turnaround; turnaround − burst = waiting. SJF sorts by burst; RR slices by quantum.
explanation: Steps: 1) list arrival+burst, 2) draw timeline, 3) record completion, 4) compute turnaround then waiting, 5) average. SJF is optimal for average waiting among non-preemptive policies with simultaneous arrival. RR waiting depends on quantum and interleaving — simulate slice by slice.
example: Bursts 4,7,9 at 0, SJF order 4,7,9. Completion 4,11,20. Waiting 0,4,11. Avg 5 ms. Same numbers under FCFS arrival order give a different average — always check the policy first.
revisionNotes: Waiting = start − arrival when single run

subject: Databases (DBMS)
title: Normalization: FDs, Keys, 2NF/3NF/BCNF
description: Closures, candidate keys and normal forms from functional dependencies.
intro: Normalization questions give FDs and ask for keys or highest normal form. Closure is the engine.
concept: X+ is everything X determines. A candidate key is a minimal determinant of all attributes. 2NF bans partial dependency on key; 3NF bans transitive via non-prime; BCNF requires every determinant to be a superkey.
explanation: Compute closures left to right. Find keys by testing minimal sets. Then check: partial? → not 2NF. Transitive via non-prime? → not 3NF. Non-superkey determinant? → not BCNF. BCNF ⇒ 3NF ⇒ 2NF.
example: R(A,B,C,D), {A→B,B→C,C→D}. A+ = ABCD so A is key. B+ misses A. Only A is candidate key.
mistakes: Calling any superkey a candidate key

subject: Computer Networks
title: IPv4 Subnetting
description: CIDR, host counts, network/broadcast and special addresses.
intro: A /n prefix leaves 32−n host bits. Subtract network and broadcast for usable hosts.
concept: Addresses = 2^hostbits. Usable = addresses − 2 (except /31,/32 edge cases). Network = all-zero host part; broadcast = all-one.
explanation: /26 → 6 host bits → 64 addresses → 62 usable. /25 → 126 usable. Loopback (127/8), network and broadcast are not ordinary host assignments.

subject: Algorithms
title: Asymptotics & Recurrences
description: Big-O thinking, quicksort worst case, recurrence solving.
intro: GATE asks for worst-case bounds and recurrence solutions, not just definitions.
concept: Fixed-pivot quicksort on sorted input partitions 0 / n−1 each time → O(n²). T(n)=2T(n/2)+n log n sums to Θ(n log² n).
explanation: Draw the recursion tree: cost per level × number of levels. For quicksort, unbalanced partitions give arithmetic-series sum. Random pivot avoids the trap.
example: T(n)=T(n−1)+O(n) ⇒ O(n²). Sorted + first-element pivot triggers it.
formulas: Worst quicksort O(n²), avg O(n log n)
mistakes: Applying Master blindly with extra log factor
revisionNotes: Pivot rule decides quicksort worst case
n log n per level × log n levels = n log² n

subject: Networks, Signals and Systems
title: LTI Systems & BIBO Stability
description: Impulse response, poles, stability and steady-state reading.
intro: Stability is about the impulse response being absolutely integrable — poles in the left-half plane for rational causal systems.
concept: BIBO ⇔ ∫|h|<∞. Zero at origin kills DC gain. Final-value theorem needs stability first.
explanation: Check poles before applying final value. Imaginary-axis poles → marginal, not BIBO. LHP strictly → stable.
example: H with zero at 0: H(0)=0 so step steady-state 0 despite stability.
mistakes: Confusing bounded step with BIBO proof

subject: Electric Circuits & Networks
title: KCL/KVL, Series-Parallel, Power
description: Ohm's law drills, equivalents and power arithmetic.
intro: Speed and unit discipline. Parallel: product over sum (two resistors).
concept: Series adds R; parallel conducts add G. P=V²/R=I²R.
explanation: 10 V over 5 Ω → 2 A. 4‖6 = 2.4 Ω. Three 6 Ω in parallel over 12 V → 72 W.
example: P = 144/2 = 72 W for Req=2 Ω at 12 V.
mistakes: Power with wrong R (total vs branch)

subject: Machine Learning
title: Evaluation: Imbalance & Cross-Validation
description: Why accuracy misleads and how CV bias/variance trades.
intro: 99% negative? All-negative scores 99% accuracy and learns nothing.
concept: Use PR/F1 for minority class. Larger k → less bias, more variance.
explanation: Pick metric for the minority class first. Report both bias and variance reasoning for CV questions.

subject: General Aptitude
title: Speed, Distance, Percentages
intro: Convert km/h to m/s (×5/18). Train problems add lengths.
concept: Distance = speed × time for (train+bridge). Successive ×, not +.
explanation: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. 22 s → 440 m minus bridge 240 = train 200 m. 10% then 20% → 0.9×0.8=0.72 → 28% off.
